title: The King and the Poor Brahmin
summary: Akbar forgets a casual promise of reward made to an impoverished scholar during a hunt. Birbal uses a crooked camel's neck to jog the royal memory.
keywords: the king and the poor brahmin
full_text:
While hunting in the wilderness six months earlier, Emperor Akbar's horse threw a shoe near a lonely hermitage. An elderly, impoverished Brahmin scholar named Devadatta welcomed the weary, disguised monarch, offered him sweet well water and fresh chapatis, and recited uplifting Sanskrit philosophical verses to ease his exhaustion.

Delighted by the scholar's hospitality, Akbar said before riding away: 'I am Emperor Akbar of Agra! Visit my court next month, and I shall bestow upon you a jagir of fertile land and five hundred gold coins!'

Overjoyed, the poor scholar sold his only milk cow to buy a clean white dhoti and traveled to Agra. However, arriving at the grand palace, Akbar was occupied with state treaties and military rebellions, and the guards repeatedly turned the old scholar away. Devadatta spent all his money and was reduced to begging on the city streets.

Desperate, the scholar approached Birbal and recounted the forgotten imperial promise.

Birbal felt deep sympathy: 'Do not worry, friend. The Emperor has not broken faith; he has merely forgotten in the rush of state affairs. I shall remind him today.'

That afternoon, Akbar and Birbal were strolling along the riverbank when they passed a camel caravan. One of the camels had a notoriously twisted, crooked neck that bent sharply to the left.

Akbar smiled and asked idly: 'Birbal, why is that camel's neck so crooked?'

Birbal sighed with deep solemnity:

'Sire, that camel was an emperor in its previous life! It made a sacred promise of a reward to a poor Brahmin, and then completely forgot its word! Because it broke its royal promise, heaven twisted its neck as a mark of shame for all eternity!'

Akbar stopped dead in his tracks. His face flushed bright crimson. The memory of the poor scholar at the hermitage came rushing back into his mind with the force of a thunderbolt!

'Birbal,' Akbar whispered, embarrassed, 'has that poor Brahmin scholar come to Agra?'

'He has been waiting outside your palace gates for three weeks, Sire, starving and without a single copper coin.'

Akbar immediately sent royal palanquins to bring Devadatta to court. The Emperor personally seated the scholar upon a velvet cushion, apologized for his forgetfulness, and granted him double the promised reward: two fertile villages, a thousand gold coins, and a royal pension for life.

Akbar embraced Birbal: 'Thank you for saving my neck from becoming as crooked as that camel's!'
